newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CEA reform will drift without consensus - Lugar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CEA reform will drift without consensus - Lugar.

text.p: Modernization of the U.S. law regulating the futures industry could "drift" without action until decade's end, Senator Richard Lugar warned Wednesday, because no one agrees on reforms to be made.
"That one is not near consensus," Lugar, chairman of the Agriculture Committee, said when reporters asked about progress on a bill to update the Commodity Exchange Act.

Three major disputes were involved -- boundaries of the so-called Treasury amendment, regulation of hybrid instruments called derivatives and creation of professionals-only markets for sophisticated and deep-pockets investors.
Lugar said senators were not going to act unless there was accord among the interested parties.
"It will drift," Lugar said, referring to the package of proposed reforms and might not be be taken up until 2000 when the Commodity Futures Trading Commission must be reauthorized.
In recent weeks, commodity exchanges have developed disputes with each other over the legislation.

In addition, the Clinton administration has not resolved an internal debate over the Treasury amendment, which exempts interbank trading in foreign exchange from CFTC oversight. CFTC alleges the exemption has been abused. There also is disagreement over the degree of regulation for derivatives.
"It's not brimming with optimism," Lugar said when asked if he was pessimistic about the legislation. He said the Senate would be in session until fall, so action was possible.
An aide said Lugar continued to seek consensus on a bill. The legislation was not moribund, the aide said, but "the situation hasn't gotten better."
